title: The Falcon Folds Its Wings
hookLine: deep sleep leaves nothing to tell at breakfast; Yajnavalkya describes it anyway, with a falcon, and finds the self under every role
carry: atman rests beneath every role you play
tomorrow: Indra called deep sleep nothing. was he right?

cards: Deep sleep is the one part of the night with nothing to report. No dream to tell over breakfast. Just a gap, and then the alarm.
A gap seems an odd thing to teach. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tries anyway. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, has walked through waking and through dreams.
Now he goes one step further down, and to describe it, he reaches for a bird. Today, the sleep with no dreams in it.

teach.b: Here's the bird, paraphrased. A falcon, or an eagle, has been flying in the open sky. It's tired, so it folds its wings and drops to its nest.
In the same way, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, he wants nothing at all and sees no dream. Then Yajnavalkya says something stranger.

teach.h: A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER
teach.b: There, a father is not a father, a mother is not a mother. The worlds are not worlds, the gods not gods, the Vedas not Vedas. A thief is not a thief.
He is untouched by good and untouched by evil, the text says, for he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. Three things. First, the folded wings.
The falcon isn't defeated. It flew all day; folding the wings is just the other half of flying. Second, the roles.
Every name a person carries by day, parent, worker, friend, even the one with a past, is set down in deep sleep. Not erased. Set down.
And here is the teaching, named plainly: the self, atman, is not any of those roles. It carries them by day, and it's what remains when they're put down. Third, the sorrows of the heart.
The text doesn't say grief is cured, only that, in that state, the sleeper has crossed over it.
And for honesty: Yajnavalkya isn't saying the goal of life is to sleep well. Deep sleep, for him, is a clue, a nightly taste of the self without wanting.
The Mandukya Upanishad lines up waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and points past all of them.

how: Vedanta teachers study deep, dreamless sleep, sushupti, beside waking and dreaming, and read Yajnavalkya's falcon as a picture of the self at rest.

o: a deep trance reached only by monks after long practice
a blank where the self is lost until the alarm rings
a nest where every name is set down and nothing is wanted

games.q: the falcon and the deep sleep — tap the pairs.
p: folds its wings and drops to its nest
a father is not a father
wants nothing and sees no dream

s: in the Brihadaranyaka, in deep sleep a thief is not a thief
father, mother, worlds, gods, thief: none of the day's names hold there.
deep sleep, in this passage, is full of dreams
asleep there, a person wants nothing at all and sees no dream.
Yajnavalkya teaches that sleeping well is the goal of life
deep sleep is a clue for him, a nightly taste of being without wanting.

games.q: you're the falcon. you've flown the open sky all day and you're tired. what do you do?
o: fold your wings and go down to your nest.
games.why: the falcon folds its wings and goes to its nest. so a person hurries, the text says, toward the sleep where he wants nothing and sees no dream.

practice: Name, silently, one role you carried today, parent, worker, friend, student, the one who has to answer, and with the next breath out set it down beside you, not thrown away, just put down.
Then the next, and when there are no more names, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, rest in prayer there.

wordCard.voice: Sleep. In deep sleep, the Brihadaranyaka says, a person wants nothing, sees no dream, and has crossed the sorrows of the heart, like a falcon folding its wings. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit sushupti: deep, dreamless sleep, the name later Vedanta teachers give the state this passage describes.

carryVoice: Your line: atman rests beneath every role you play. Every name is set down at night, and the self is still there. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.19 (the tired falcon or eagle folds its wings and goes to its nest; the sleeper desires no desire, sees no dream)

Mandukya Upanishad 3–7 (waking, dreaming, deep sleep and the fourth)
